unit.title: Implement and maintain internal control procedures

summary: This unit teaches you to put internal controls in place and keep them working in a Jamaican business or public body. You will learn what internal control is, how to assess risk, which controls protect purchasing, payroll, cash, stock and assets, how to document and introduce procedures, how to test that controls work, and what to do when they fail or when someone tries to override them.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is written for supervisors and managers in Jamaican businesses, hotels, schools and public bodies who are responsible for protecting money, goods and records, and for making sure that work is done the way the organisation intends. You will **implement** controls (design them, write them down, introduce them) and **maintain** them (monitor, test, report weaknesses and put them right).

**Internal control** is the set of policies, procedures and checks that an organisation builds into its daily work to give **reasonable assurance** that its assets are protected, its records are reliable, it obeys the law and its own rules, and its work is done efficiently. Notice the words 'reasonable assurance': no system can guarantee that error or fraud will never happen. Good controls make them less likely and make them easier to find.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workplace
rows: Explain internal control
State its purpose, its main parts and who is responsible for it, and why the attitude of senior managers matters.
Assess risk
List what could go wrong in a process, score each risk for likelihood and impact, rank them and decide how much control each deserves.
Choose and design controls
Select preventive, detective and corrective controls for purchasing, payroll, cash, sales, stock, assets and IT; separate duties; set approval limits.
Document and introduce controls
Write procedures, map processes, build a risk and control matrix, train staff and explain why the controls matter.
Monitor and test controls
Review exception reports, reconcile records, test samples, calculate exception rates and follow up.
Deal with weaknesses
Find the cause of a failure, fix it, report it to the right people and track the action to completion.
Reduce the risk of fraud
Recognise the conditions and warning signs of fraud, and support a safe way for staff to report concerns.
Review and maintain controls
Update controls when systems, people or risks change, and judge whether a control is worth its cost.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario questions and short calculations (percentages, scores, differences).
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as three-way match, walkthrough, compensating control) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practical tasks**: mapping a purchasing process and building a risk and control matrix; testing a sample of payment files, reporting the results and agreeing actions with a 'finance manager'.

blocks.note: Learn the key terms in the Revision section. In scenario questions, ask three things: what could go wrong, which control would stop or catch it, and who should do it.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: What internal control is and who is responsible

blocks.p: Internal control has four broad aims. Every control you meet in this unit serves at least one of them.

head: Aim
What it means
Example
rows: Protect assets
Cash, stock, vehicles, equipment and information are not lost, stolen or misused
Locked stores, a safe with a key log, tagged laptops
Reliable records
Accounts and reports are accurate, complete and on time, so decisions rest on true figures
Reconciling the ledger to supplier statements
Compliance
Laws, regulations, contracts and the organisation's own policies are followed
Following public procurement rules; paying statutory deductions on time
Efficiency and effectiveness
Resources are used well and the organisation's aims are met
Automated matching that saves clerks' time

blocks.h: The five parts of an internal control system

blocks.p: A widely used model describes five connected parts. They must all be present and working together; strong checks mean little if managers ignore them.

head: Part
What it is
Example in a Jamaican organisation
rows: Control environment
The attitude and example of the owners, board and managers; the code of conduct; clear roles and responsibilities; the competence of staff
A chief executive who has her own expense claims approved by the chair
A signed code of conduct for every new employee
Risk assessment
Identifying what could stop the organisation meeting its aims and judging how likely and how serious each risk is
A risk register for a municipal corporation's procurement process
Control activities
The checks and procedures themselves: approvals, separation of duties, reconciliations, access limits, physical security
Two signatures on every payment above a set amount
Information and communication
Written procedures, accurate reports, and clear ways to pass problems upward
A procedures manual; an exception report; a confidential reporting line
Monitoring
Ongoing checking that controls still work, and reporting weaknesses to those who can fix them
Quarterly sample testing; internal audit reports to the audit committee

blocks.note: The **control environment** is the foundation. Staff copy what leaders do, not what they say. If a director skips approvals to 'get things done', the other four parts will weaken, because everyone learns that rules are optional. This is called weak **tone at the top**.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Who
Responsibility
rows: Management (owners, chief executive, department heads)
Designs, introduces and maintains internal control. It is management's job, and it cannot be handed over to the auditors.
Every employee
Follows the procedures, reports errors and concerns, and does not override controls.
Board or audit committee
Oversees the control system, receives reports on weaknesses and fraud, and makes sure action is taken.
Internal audit
Tests and reports on controls **independently**, and recommends improvements. It does not run the controls for management.
External auditor
Gives an opinion on the financial statements and may report control weaknesses noticed, but is not responsible for the organisation's controls.

ul: Controls give **reasonable**, not absolute, assurance.
Two or more people working together (**collusion**) can defeat controls that depend on separation of duties.
Managers can **override** controls. This is why the control environment matters and why overrides must be reported.
Human error, tiredness and poor training can make a good control fail.
Controls cost money and time. A control is worth having only if its benefit is greater than its cost.

blocks.h: Is the control worth its cost?

blocks.p: A manager decides how much control is enough by comparing the cost of a control with the loss it is expected to prevent. **Expected annual loss = likelihood (how often) × impact (how much)**.

**Worked example.** A distributor expects to lose about J$900,000 a year to duplicate payments. A new automatic duplicate-invoice check costs J$240,000 a year to run and is expected to cut the expected loss to J$300,000. Benefit = J$900,000 − J$300,000 = J$600,000. Net benefit = J$600,000 − J$240,000 = **J$360,000 a year**, so the control is worth having. If the same control cost J$700,000 a year, it would cost more than the J$600,000 it saves, and the manager should look for a cheaper way.

blocks.note: Do not forget **hidden costs**: delays, frustrated customers and staff, and extra approvals that people learn to get round. Put high-value controls where the risk is highest (payments, payroll, cash) and keep controls light on low risks such as small stationery purchases.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: You cannot design good controls until you know what they are for. The first step is to find **what could go wrong** in each process and **how badly**, then decide what to do about it.

flow: Identify the process and its objectives (what must be achieved)
List what could go wrong at each step: error, theft, delay, breaking the law, system failure
Score each risk for likelihood and for impact, and multiply to get a risk score
Rank the risks, highest score first
Decide the response: reduce (add controls), transfer (insure, contract out), avoid (stop the activity) or accept (tolerate and monitor)
Record everything in a risk register with a named owner
Review the scores after the controls are in place and whenever things change

blocks.p: Many organisations use a scale of 1 to 5 for each. Your organisation may use different words or bands; follow its scale.

head: Score
Likelihood (how often)
Impact (how serious)
rows: Rare: not expected in years
Minor: small cost, no lasting effect
Unlikely: perhaps once in several years
Moderate: small loss or short delay
Possible: about once a year
Significant: noticeable loss; some reputation damage
Likely: several times a year
Major: large loss; service stops for a time
Almost certain: monthly or more
Severe: very large loss; legal action or closure

blocks.p: **Risk score = likelihood × impact**, so the highest possible score is 25. A typical example of bands: 1 to 5 low, 6 to 10 medium, 11 to 15 high, 16 to 25 very high.
**Worked example.** A Kingston bakery chain starts taking orders online. The manager scores four risks:

head: Risk
Likelihood
Impact
Score
Rank
rows: Card payment fraud
1st
Ingredients spoiled by over-ordering
2nd
Wrong orders keyed in
3rd= (tied)
Website down at peak time
3rd= (tied)

blocks.p: Payment fraud scores highest even though it is not the most frequent, because one large loss could hurt the business badly. The manager would put the strongest controls there first.

ul: **Inherent risk** is the risk before any control is applied.
**Residual risk** is what remains after controls. If a new control cuts the likelihood of card fraud from 3 to 1, the residual score is 1 × 5 = **5**, down from 15.
Management decides how much residual risk it will accept. This is its **risk appetite**. Public bodies and banks usually accept less than a small trader.

blocks.h: The risk register and the risk and control matrix

blocks.p: A **risk register** lists each risk, its score, its owner and the planned response. A **risk and control matrix** goes one step further: for each step of a process it shows the risk, the existing control, any **gap** (where there is no control, or it is weak), the recommended control and the person responsible. You will build one in the group practical.

head: Process step
Risk
Existing control
Gap
Recommended control
Owner
rows: Change a supplier's bank details
Payments diverted to a false account
None; the accounts clerk makes the change on an email
No check and no independence
Change only after a call-back to the number on file; second person approves; weekly report of changes reviewed
Finance manager

blocks.note: Work from the highest risk down. A matrix that adds an approval to every step is a sign of poor judgement: look at cost and practicality too.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Types of control and separation of duties

head: Type
Purpose
Examples
rows: Preventive
Stops an error or fraud before it happens
Approval before a purchase order is issued; passwords; locked stores; approved supplier list; system blocks a payment above a user's limit
Detective
Finds an error or fraud after it has happened
Reconciliations; supplier statement checks; stock counts; exception reports; review of the audit trail
Corrective
Puts things right after a problem is found and stops it recurring
Restoring data from a back-up; recovering an overpayment; changing a procedure after an audit finding; retraining staff

blocks.p: A good system uses all three. Preventive controls are usually cheapest in the long run, but no set of them is perfect, so detective controls catch what slips through and corrective controls repair the damage.

head: Point
Manual control
Automated control
rows: How it works
A person does the check (signs, counts, compares)
The system does it (a limit, a required field, a block, a duplicate-invoice check)
Strength
Uses judgement; needs no software
Works the same way every time; fast; leaves an audit trail
Weakness
Can be skipped, rushed or forgotten
Only as good as its settings; can be switched off by someone with access

blocks.note: Automated controls still need maintenance. Control who can change the settings, and test them after every system change.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: No one person should control all stages of a transaction. If one person can **authorise** it, **record** it, **hold the asset** and **reconcile** it, that person can commit an error or fraud and hide it. Split these four functions between different people.

head: Function
Example in purchasing
Example in payroll
rows: Authorise
Manager approves the purchase order
HR approves a new starter and a pay change
Record
Accounts payable enters the invoice
Payroll enters hours and calculates pay
Hold or handle the asset
Stores receives the goods; finance releases the payment
Cashier or bank releases pay
Reconcile or review
Someone independent compares the ledger to supplier statements
A senior officer compares this month's pay run to last month's

blocks.h: When duties cannot be separated: compensating controls

blocks.p: A small business in, say, Ocho Rios or Mandeville may have only two or three office staff. Duties then cannot be fully separated. The answer is not to ignore the problem but to add a **compensating control**: a check that makes up for the weakness. Typical examples:

ul: The **owner or manager** reviews the bank statements, the bank reconciliation and key reports each month.
The owner personally signs cheques or approves online payments, with supporting documents attached.
A person from outside the team (a part-time accountant, a board member) performs surprise counts and checks supplier statements.
**Mandatory leave**: staff in sensitive roles must take their leave, and someone else does their work. Many frauds are found when the person is away.

blocks.p: An **authorisation matrix** (also called a delegation or approval-limits table) shows which role may approve which transactions up to what amount. It must be written, approved by the board or chief executive and kept current.

head: Role
May approve purchases up to
Notes
rows: Supervisor
Within budget; not own purchases
Department manager
Quotations needed above J$250,000 (example)
Finance director
Counter-signed by chief executive above this
Chief executive / board
Board minute for very large items

ul: Nobody approves their own expenses or purchases.
Splitting one purchase into smaller ones to stay under a limit is a breach of the control and a warning sign.
Public bodies must also follow national public procurement rules. The matrix adds local detail; it cannot be looser than those rules.

blocks.p: This section gives the controls you are expected to know for the main business cycles. For each, think: what could go wrong, and which control stops or catches it?

flow: Need identified; requisition raised and approved by the budget holder
Supplier chosen from the approved supplier list (quotations or tender as the rules require)
Numbered purchase order approved within the authorisation limits
Goods received by stores, checked against the order, and a goods received note (GRN) completed
Accounts payable matches the order, the GRN and the supplier's invoice (**three-way match**); differences are queried
Payment prepared from approved, matched invoices only; released by authorised signatories (usually two)
Monthly reconciliation of supplier statements to the ledger; exception report reviewed

ul: **Approved supplier list:** new suppliers are checked and approved by someone outside the buying team.

**Supplier master file:** changes to bank details are made only after confirming the request by phone using a number **already on file**, never one in the email asking for the change. A second person approves the change, and a report of all changes is reviewed weekly. Email requests to change bank details are a common fraud.

**Three-way match:** do not pay an invoice for more than was ordered and received. If the invoice shows 120 units but only 100 were ordered and received, pay for 100 (or hold the invoice) and ask the supplier for a credit note.
**Duplicate payments:** the system or the clerk checks the invoice number, supplier and amount before paying.
**Only HR** creates employees, changes pay rates or records leavers, on signed, approved documents. **Payroll staff process pay but cannot create employees.**
A **change report** lists every starter, leaver and pay change since the last run, and a senior officer checks it to source documents before each pay run.
Hours, overtime and allowances are approved by line managers before payment.
Each pay run is **compared with the last one** and large differences are explained.
Pay goes by bank transfer to an account in the employee's own name. Changes of bank details are confirmed with the employee directly.

Occasionally check that everyone paid is a real person in post (a **payroll verification** or headcount, managers confirming their staff lists). A person who is paid but does not work for the organisation is a **ghost employee**.
Unique log-ins and an audit trail on the payroll system.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** Payroll was J$18,420,000 in January and J$19,610,000 in February. The difference is J$19,610,000 − J$18,420,000 = J$1,190,000, which is about 6.5% of January's figure (1,190,000 ÷ 18,420,000). HR confirms that three approved appointments account for J$410,000. That leaves **J$780,000 unexplained** to investigate (J$1,190,000 − J$410,000).

ul: **Receive:** use pre-numbered receipt books or till rolls; account for every number. A missing or spoiled number must be explained and signed off.
**Post and counter cash:** two people open the post and list cheques and cash received, and both sign the list.
**Record:** the person who handles the cash is not the person who posts the cash book or does the reconciliation.
**Bank intact and daily:** takings are banked in full, as soon as practicable, never used to pay expenses or 'borrowed'. Banking intact means the deposit can be matched to the receipts.
**Check:** the bank deposit slip is agreed to the till total and the cash book by someone independent. A manager does **surprise counts** of tills and petty cash.
**Safes and keys:** a few named staff hold keys or codes, with a key log. Codes are changed when staff leave.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A till opens with a float of J$10,000. The till roll shows cash sales of J$126,400. Expected cash = J$10,000 + J$126,400 = J$136,400. The cashier counts J$134,100. Shortage = J$136,400 − J$134,100 = **J$2,300**. Repeated small shortages should be investigated, not ignored.

ul: Prices come from an approved price list in the system; changes are approved.
**Credit notes and write-offs** are approved by someone outside the sales team, because sales staff could use them to hide theft or to favour a friend.
Credit limits are set by an authorised person and checked before an order is accepted.
Invoices are numbered in sequence and every number is accounted for; customer statements are sent and queries tracked.
Stock is kept locked; only stores staff have access; every movement is recorded on a document (goods received, issue note, transfer, return).
**Stock counts** (periodic, plus surprise cycle counts) are done by staff **independent of the stores**, with the storekeeper present but not counting.
Differences are investigated before the records are changed. Adjustments to stock records are approved by a manager outside the stores.
Damaged and slow-moving stock is reviewed and written off only with approval.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** The stock record shows 640 units costing J$1,150 each; the count finds 618. Shortage = 22 units. Cost = 22 × J$1,150 = **J$25,300**. As a share of the recorded quantity, 22 ÷ 640 = about **3.4%**. Check for causes first: goods received but not recorded, items issued without a note, a count in the wrong place, or theft.

ul: A **fixed asset register** lists each item above the capitalisation threshold with its tag number, description, location, custodian, cost and date bought.
Each item (laptops, vehicles, equipment) is **tagged** so it can be found and checked.
Items taken off site are signed out, and the register is checked against the real items at least once a year.
Disposals and write-offs are approved by someone senior, not by the person who has custody of the item.

head: Control
What it does
rows: Unique user log-ins and strong passwords
Every action is traceable to one person; shared passwords destroy this
Role-based access
Each user can do only what their job needs. The person entering invoices cannot approve payments or change supplier bank details.
Prompt removal and regular review of access
Access ends the day someone leaves or moves; managers review the user list every quarter
Audit trail (audit log)
A record of who made each entry or change, and when; reviewed for unusual changes
Automated controls
Payment limits, required fields, duplicate checks, blocks on unapproved suppliers; tested before use
Back-ups and recovery
Regular copies of data stored safely and tested by restoring them
Change control
System settings are changed only with approval, and the change is recorded and tested

blocks.p: A cloud accounting system gives access from anywhere, automatic updates and back-ups by the provider. It also brings risks: unauthorised access over the internet, data loss, and errors that spread quickly through linked processes. The firm still owns its controls. It should use **two-step sign-in**, control who has access, confirm the provider's security and back-up arrangements in the contract, keep its own regular export of key data, and handle personal data in line with the data protection law. **Set up and test controls before go-live**, not after.

head: Corner
Meaning
Example
What reduces it
rows: Pressure
A personal or work need
Debt; illness in the family; unrealistic targets
Fair targets; support such as an employee assistance programme
Opportunity
A weakness that lets someone commit fraud and hide it
One person controls a whole process
**Internal controls**: separation of duties, approvals, reconciliations, access limits, surprise counts
Rationalisation
A way of justifying it
'I am underpaid'; 'I will pay it back'
Code of conduct; leaders who follow the rules; prompt, fair action when fraud is found

blocks.p: Management can most directly affect **opportunity**. The belief that fraud will be found is itself a strong deterrent.

ul: A long-serving employee who never takes leave, or will not let anyone cover their work.
Staff living beyond their means; sudden changes in behaviour.
Missing documents, altered records, or a reluctance to provide them.
Purchases just below an approval limit, or many orders to one new supplier.
Complaints from suppliers about unpaid invoices that the records show as paid.
A manager who regularly overrides controls or pressures staff to skip steps.

blocks.note: A red flag is a reason to look, not proof. Do not accuse anyone. Report the concern through the proper channel and let the investigation find the facts.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Staff often see fraud first. The organisation should give them a **confidential channel** (a hotline, an email address or a named senior officer outside their line management) and protect those who use it from reprisal. A person who reports suspected wrongdoing is a **whistleblower**. Do not try to find out who made an anonymous report; investigate the facts independently of the people involved.

blocks.note: If a senior manager asks you to pay a supplier urgently and skip the usual approval, do not skip it. Follow the procedure, and refer the request to the person with authority to approve. If the manager insists, report the override to the next level, the audit committee or internal audit.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A control that exists only in someone's head disappears when that person leaves. A **procedures manual** (or standard operating procedures) makes sure that controls are applied the same way every time, helps new staff learn, and gives managers and auditors something to test against.

ul: **Purpose and scope:** what the procedure is for and whom it covers.
**Roles** by job title, not by name, so it stays valid when people change jobs.
**Numbered steps**, in order, showing who does each step, which form or screen is used and the time limits.
**Controls built in:** approvals, checks and documents, shown at the step where they happen.
A **flowchart** so that staff can see the whole process and its decisions at a glance.
**Version number, date and owner**, and one central, controlled copy so that old versions are not used.

blocks.p: To design or improve a control you must first understand the process as it really works, not as the manual says. Walk through the process with the people who do it. Draw each step in order, showing who does it and what document is created. Look for steps where one person does too much, where no one checks, or where documents are not matched.

flow: Find the risk and the gap, and agree the control with the process owner
Check that the control is practical, fits the system and costs less than the risk
Write or update the procedure, flowchart and forms; give every control an owner
Get approval from the right level (manager, finance committee or board)
Brief and train the staff who use it, explaining **why** it matters, with a quick guide and a contact person for questions
Start on a set date when forms, system settings and training are ready
Check early transactions closely, give feedback, fix steps that do not work
Test the control and review it regularly

blocks.note: People follow controls they understand. If a rule looks like pointless delay, they will find a way round it. Explain the risk, listen to their ideas and keep the control as simple as the risk allows.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Review controls **regularly** (for example every year) and **whenever the risks change**: a new system, a move to the cloud, a merger, a new product, new laws, or a weakness found by testing or audit. When moving to a new accounting system, review and set up the controls **before** go-live and test them.

head: Trigger for review
Example
rows: New system
Moving to a cloud accounting package next quarter
Change in the organisation
New branch opened; two agencies merged
Change in risk
A fraud attempt; a rise in stock losses
Finding from a test or audit
Sample testing shows missing second signatures
Change in law or rules
New procurement rules for public bodies

sections.title: Monitoring, testing and dealing with weaknesses

blocks.p: Controls decay. People change, systems change, shortcuts grow. **Monitoring** is the ongoing checking that controls are still working as intended. It has two forms: checking built into daily work (reconciliations, exception reports, supervisor review) and separate tests (sample testing, internal audit).

ul: **Reconciliations:** comparing two sets of records (the ledger and a supplier statement; the cash book and the bank statement; the stock record and the count) and explaining each difference.

**Exception reports:** a report listing only items that break a rule or limit, such as payments over J$500,000, payments without a purchase order, or changes to supplier bank details. A manager reviews it, so attention goes where it matters.
**Supervisor review:** a manager signs to show that a check was done, and keeps the evidence.

blocks.p: **Worked example of a reconciliation.** A supplier's statement shows J$845,000. The firm's ledger shows J$779,500. Difference = J$65,500. The firm finds an invoice for J$48,000 not yet recorded in the ledger, and a payment of J$17,500 that the firm made but the supplier has not yet recorded. J$48,000 + J$17,500 = J$65,500. The difference is fully explained, and the firm now records the missing invoice.

flow: Read the written procedure and list the key controls (approval, matching, signatures, access)
Do a **walkthrough**: follow one transaction through the process from start to finish to confirm the controls exist in practice
Choose a **sample** of transactions from the period (random, and including some large ones)
For each item, check the evidence: the approved order, goods received note, matched invoice, correct approver and both signatures
Record every **exception** (a case where the control was not met)
Calculate the **exception rate** for each control
Find the cause of each type of exception
Report, agree actions with owners and dates, then follow up and retest

blocks.p: **Exception rate = exceptions ÷ items tested × 100.** A test of 60 payment vouchers finds 9 without a second signature: 9 ÷ 60 = 0.15 = **15%**. Compliance rate = 100% − 15% = 85%. The test of 48 invoices with 3 unmatched gives 3 ÷ 48 = 6.25%, or about 6.3%.

blocks.note: A small number of exceptions in a sample does not prove the whole population is fine. Look at what **kind** of exceptions they are. A missing signature on a small payment is less serious than a payment released on a manager's instruction without any approval. The most serious are those that show a **control override** or possible fraud.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Do not stop at counting errors. Ask **why** the control failed. The cause shapes the fix.

head: Likely cause
Typical fix
rows: Staff did not know the rule
Training; a quick guide
The step is slow or unclear, so people skip it
Redesign the step; clearer instructions; faster approval route for urgent payments
System allows the breach
Change the system setting; add a block
Workload or staffing
Review staffing or timing
Deliberate breach or override
Report under the policy and disciplinary rules; report to the audit committee

ul: Report weaknesses to **management** and, where significant, to the **audit committee** or board.
Each recommendation needs an **action, an owner and a date**.
Keep an **action log**; report progress at each committee meeting.
**Retest** after the changes to show that the fix works.
Update the procedures manual and train staff.

blocks.p: **Worked example of prioritising.** An audit report finds three weaknesses: supplier bank details are changed with no review, the storekeeper counts stock alone, and staff share a system password. The manager fixes the bank-detail weakness first, because one fraudulent change could lead to a large payment that cannot be recovered. Then she arranges independent counts, and gives each user a unique log-in with the audit trail switched on.

Internal audit independently tests whether controls are well designed and working, and reports to management and the audit committee. Because it is independent, it cannot also operate the controls it tests. Managers use its findings to fix weaknesses.

ul: explain what internal control is, its four aims and its five parts;
explain why the control environment and tone at the top matter and what overriding a control means;
say who is responsible for internal control (management) and what internal audit and the audit committee do;
score risks as likelihood × impact, rank them, and explain inherent and residual risk;
compare the cost of a control with the loss it prevents;
tell preventive, detective and corrective controls apart, and manual from automated;
separate authorising, recording, holding assets and reconciling, and use a compensating control where that is not possible;
set up approval limits in an authorisation matrix;
describe the controls over purchasing, payroll, cash, sales, stock, fixed assets and IT;
carry out a three-way match and a supplier reconciliation, and work out a cash or stock shortage;
recognise the fraud triangle and warning signs, and explain why a confidential reporting channel is needed;
write a procedure, draw a flowchart and build a risk and control matrix;
introduce a control with training and explain why it matters;
test a control with a walkthrough and a sample, and calculate the exception rate;
find the cause of a weakness, report it, agree actions with owners and dates, and follow up;
decide when controls must be reviewed.

terms: Policies, procedures and checks that give reasonable assurance that assets are safe, records are reliable, rules are followed and work is efficient
The attitude, example and standards of the owners and managers; the foundation of the other parts
The attitude of senior leaders to honesty and rules, which staff copy
Risk before controls / risk left after controls
A list of risks with scores, owners and responses
A table linking each risk in a process to its control, any gap, the recommended control and the owner
Stops an error or fraud before it happens
Finds an error or fraud after it has happened
Puts things right after a problem is found
Splitting authorising, recording, handling assets and reconciling between different people
A check that makes up for a weakness elsewhere, such as an owner's review where duties cannot be separated
A table of which roles may approve what, up to what amount
Checking the purchase order, goods received note and supplier invoice against each other before payment
Comparing two sets of records and explaining each difference
A report listing only items that break a rule or limit
Following one transaction through a process from start to finish to see that the controls work
A system record of who made each entry or change, and when
An unannounced count of cash or stock to check it agrees with the records
A rule that staff in sensitive roles must take their leave so that others cover their work
Pressure, opportunity and rationalisation: the three conditions for fraud
A person who reports suspected wrongdoing through a protected channel
A person on the payroll who does not work for the organisation
Ongoing checking that controls still work as intended

c1.title: Till shortages at a hardware store in Mandeville
c1.text: Beverley Grant owns a hardware store in Mandeville with four staff: a manager, two cashiers, and a bookkeeper who comes in three days a week. Dwight, a cashier of six years, takes the cash at the till, writes up the cash book each evening and takes the deposit to the bank. He has not taken his annual leave in four years. Small shortages of J$1,000 to J$3,000 appear in his till most weeks. Ms Grant asks you, as a consultant, to advise her.

c2.title: A payroll increase at a municipal corporation in St Ann
c2.text: A municipal corporation in St Ann has 220 staff. The payroll clerk, Marcia, can add new employees, change pay rates and bank details, and run the monthly pay. This year the finance officer compares each pay run with the one before. January's payroll was J$18,420,000 and February's was J$19,610,000. HR confirms that three approved appointments started in February at a total monthly cost of J$410,000.

c3.title: Stock and assets at a building-supply warehouse in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: A building-supply warehouse in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, keeps its stock records on a computer. The storekeeper, Mr Reid, receives goods, issues goods, updates the records and also does the year-end stock count on his own. The record for one type of cement-block pallet shows 640 units costing J$1,150 each, but the count finds 618. Separately, a laptop on the asset list was found at a manager's house; the asset list shows no location or custodian.

c4.title: Online orders at a bakery chain in Kingston
c4.text: A bakery chain in Kingston is about to take orders and card payments on its website. The finance manager scores four risks, each for likelihood and impact on a scale of 1 to 5. Card payment fraud: likelihood 3, impact 5. Ingredients spoiled through over-ordering: likelihood 4, impact 3. Wrong orders keyed in: likelihood 4, impact 2. Website down at peak time: likelihood 2, impact 4. A fraud-screening tool would cost J$300,000 a year to run and is expected to cut the expected yearly fraud loss from J$900,000 to J$400,000.

c5.title: Internal audit findings at an agency in May Pen
c5.text: The internal auditor of a statutory agency in May Pen tests 60 payment vouchers and finds that 9 have only one signature, although the procedure needs two. Seven of the nine were 'urgent' payments that the finance director told staff to release without waiting for the second signatory. An officer, Kerry-Ann, later sends a confidential note to the audit committee chair saying she is worried about this practice.

questions.q: Which weakness in Dwight's work is the most serious from a control point of view?
o: He has served six years, so his knowledge of the till is too specialised to replace
The cash book is written up in the evening rather than during the trading day
One person receives the cash, records it and banks it, so no one can check
The shortages are small, so they are probably counting errors that will even out
questions.why: Receiving, recording and banking the cash are separate functions that should be done by different people. When one person does all three, errors or theft can be hidden. Small shortages that recur should be investigated, not dismissed.

questions.q: With only four staff, duties cannot be fully separated. Which action would best compensate?
o: The owner agrees the till total, cash book and deposit slip, and does surprise counts
The other cashier adds a second signature to the cash book each evening, working at the next till
Dwight counts the takings twice before banking and signs the count sheet each time
The cash book moves to the bookkeeper, who works in the store only three days a week
questions.why: A compensating control is an independent check that makes up for the weakness. A review by the owner or manager, with surprise counts, gives the independence that separation of duties would have given. Asking the same person to count twice adds no independence.

questions.q: Dwight says he never takes leave because 'the till would fall apart'. What should Ms Grant do?
o: Accept this as loyalty and offer him a cash bonus in place of taking his annual leave
Dismiss him at once, since refusing leave is proof that he is stealing
Let him take leave only in weeks when the owner is away from the store
Require him to take his leave, with someone else covering the till and cash book
questions.why: A mandatory leave rule lets another person see how the work is really done, and many problems appear while the usual person is away. It is a control, not an accusation. Refusing leave is a warning sign, not proof of fraud.

questions.q: One evening the till roll shows cash sales of J$126,400 and the float is J$10,000. Dwight counts J$134,100. What is the shortage?
questions.why: Expected cash = float + cash sales = J$10,000 + J$126,400 = J$136,400. The shortage is J$136,400 - J$134,100 = J$2,300. Forgetting the float gives a wrong answer.

questions.q: The comparison of this month's payroll with last month's is an example of which type of control?
o: A preventive control, as it stops anyone being paid wrongly in the first place
A detective control, as it finds problems after they have happened
A corrective control, as it repairs the payroll data when an error is found
An automated control, as it needs no manager to review the result
questions.why: The comparison is made after the pay run and spots unusual differences, so it detects problems; it does not stop them. A manager must still review and explain the result. Correction comes only after the cause is found.

questions.q: How much of the increase between January and February is still unexplained after the approved appointments are allowed for?
questions.why: The total increase is J$19,610,000 - J$18,420,000 = J$1,190,000. The approved appointments explain J$410,000, leaving J$780,000 to investigate for errors, unapproved additions or ghost employees.

questions.q: Which change would best prevent a ghost employee being added in future?
o: Only HR may create employees or change pay; payroll may not edit the employee file
The payroll clerk checks her own additions against the change report before it goes to payment
The payroll system is backed up every evening and a copy is stored off site
All new employees are paid by cheque rather than by transfer to a bank account
questions.why: Separating HR (who authorise changes) from payroll (who process pay) means no one person can create an employee and pay them. A clerk checking her own additions is no independent check, and back-ups do not control who adds records.

questions.q: Finance suspects that some of the extra J$780,000 is paid to people who do not work for the agency. What is the best next step?
o: Ask Marcia to explain each addition over the phone and accept her explanation as sufficient evidence
Reduce every employee's pay slightly until the difference disappears from the payroll
Trace each addition since January to appointment papers and confirm the person is in post
Wait until the next pay run to see whether the same difference appears a second time
questions.why: A payroll verification traces each addition to source documents and to a real person in post. Asking only the person with access may warn her, and cutting everyone's pay would punish innocent staff. Keep evidence safe and report to senior management and internal audit.

questions.q: What is the cost of the stock shortage on the cement-block pallets?
questions.why: The shortage is 640 - 618 = 22 units. At J$1,150 each, the cost is 22 x J$1,150 = J$25,300. J$736,000 is the whole recorded stock (640 x J$1,150), and J$710,700 is the value of the stock counted (618 x J$1,150), so neither is the shortage.

questions.q: Which change would make the stock count a stronger control?
o: Staff from outside the stores count, and differences are investigated before records change
The storekeeper counts a second time and signs the sheet to confirm his first figure
The count is done once a year, on a fixed date that is announced to the stores staff well in advance
The storekeeper adjusts the record to the count and reports the adjustment afterwards
questions.why: An independent count removes the conflict of interest in the storekeeper checking his own work. Differences must be investigated first (unrecorded issues, wrong location, theft) and adjustments approved by someone outside the stores.

questions.q: What is the best response to the laptop found at the manager's house?
o: Remove the laptop from the asset list, since it is no longer kept in the office
Ask the manager to buy the laptop at its depreciated value to settle the matter
Add a note to the register about this laptop and leave all other assets as they are
Tag assets, record who has each one and where, and check the register every year
questions.why: A fixed asset register is a control only if each item can be found and a person is accountable for it. Tagging, location, custodian, sign-out and an annual check against real items make loss or private use visible.

questions.q: Using the scores, what is the residual risk score for card payment fraud if the screening tool cuts the likelihood from 3 to 1 and the impact stays at 5?
questions.why: Risk score = likelihood x impact. After the control: 1 x 5 = 5. The original (inherent) score was 3 x 5 = 15. The remaining risk after controls is called residual risk.

questions.q: Which two risks have the same score, and what does this mean for the order of control work?
o: Spoiled ingredients and website down both score 12, so both must be solved before fraud
Wrong orders and website down both score 8, so cost and practicality decide between them
Card fraud and spoiled ingredients both score 15, so they have equal priority for controls
Wrong orders and card fraud both score 10, so controls on both can safely wait a year
questions.why: Wrong orders (4 x 2) and website down (2 x 4) both equal 8. Tied risks are ranked by judgement: cost of control, practicality and the type of harm. Fraud (15) and spoilage (12) rank higher.

questions.q: Should the bakery buy the fraud-screening tool, judging only by cost and benefit?
o: No: it costs J$300,000 a year, which is less than the J$400,000 of expected loss that still remains
Yes: it removes all fraud risk from the website, so any cost would be worth paying
No: automated controls need no cost-benefit test because the system does the work
Yes: it saves J$500,000 a year in expected loss for J$300,000, a net benefit of J$200,000
questions.why: Expected loss falls by J$900,000 - J$400,000 = J$500,000. Net benefit = J$500,000 - J$300,000 = J$200,000. The tool does not remove all risk, so cost and benefit must be compared, and the remaining J$400,000 must still be managed.

questions.q: Each morning the manager reviews a system report of every refund over J$10,000 on the website. What kind of report is this?
o: An exception report, which lists only items above a limit
A reconciliation, which compares two complete sets of records line by line
A risk register, which lists each risk with its score, owner and response
A walkthrough, which follows one order through the system from start to end
questions.why: An exception report lists only the items that break a limit or rule, so the manager's attention goes where the risk is. A reconciliation compares two sets of records, and a walkthrough follows one transaction through a process.

questions.q: What is the exception rate for the missing second signature?
questions.why: Exception rate = exceptions / items tested x 100 = 9 / 60 x 100 = 15%. The compliance rate is the opposite figure, 85%. The rate by itself does not tell you how serious the breaches are.

questions.q: Seven of the nine exceptions were released on the finance director's instruction. How should the auditor treat this?
o: As a staffing problem, to be solved by retraining the payment clerks in the procedure
As acceptable, because the director has authority to approve any payment he chooses
As a control override by senior management, reported to the audit committee
As a matter only for the director, since he is the person who gave the instruction
questions.why: When a senior manager directs staff to bypass a control, the weakness lies in the control environment, not in staff knowledge. A report only to the person responsible would not be independent, so it goes to the audit committee.

questions.q: How should the audit committee chair deal with Kerry-Ann's confidential note?
o: Protect her identity and have the matter looked into independently of the finance director
Tell the finance director who sent the note so that he can answer her concern directly himself
Set it aside, because a note that is not from a manager does not need action
Ask other staff in the department whether they agree with what she has written
questions.why: Staff are more likely to report concerns if they are protected. The matter should be investigated by someone independent of those involved, and reprisals avoided. Revealing her name would put her at risk and discourage others.

questions.q: An invoice for 120 units arrives, but the purchase order and goods received note both show 100 units. What should the accounts payable officer do?
o: Pay the invoice in full now and recover the difference from the supplier's next order later
Change the purchase order to 120 units so that all three documents agree
Pay for 100 units and tell the supplier to stop sending invoices for the balance
Hold the extra 20 units and ask the supplier for a credit note or proof of delivery
questions.why: The three-way match shows the firm should pay only for what it ordered and received. Changing the order to fit the invoice destroys the control, and ignoring the difference may cause a dispute. The query is resolved with the supplier in writing.

questions.q: A finance clerk is moved to the sales team but her access to the payment approval screen stays on. What is the main risk?
o: The finance system will run more slowly because of the extra user on the licence
She could approve payments outside her new duties, and the action would look authorised
Her new manager will have to approve every payment that she later asks the clerk to make for her
Her old colleagues will have to learn how to use the system without her help
questions.why: Access rights should match a person's current role and be removed or changed promptly when she moves or leaves. A regular review of the user list catches this. Leftover access allows unauthorised actions that appear to be authorised.
